Issue specification:
 Implement the first graph-based ProjectWeave runtime
## Purpose

Implement the first ProjectWeave runtime so that the core ideas from Issue #1 work end to end using a graph-based model.

This first implementation should establish the core runtime rather than build a small one-off dispatcher.

It should support:

- using a GitHub Project as the canonical project state
- defining project-level workflows as graphs
- selecting work from the project
- treating available AI resources as graph inputs and constraints
- routing execution based on task and resource state
- dispatching work to replaceable executors
- passing structured results between nodes
- reflecting results back into GitHub

UI, daemons, multi-project coordination, and an autonomous project-manager AI are intentionally out of scope.

## Basic model

A ProjectWeave Run conceptually receives:

```text
GitHub Project
      +
Project-level Graph
      +
Resource Envelope
      ↓
ProjectWeave Runtime
      ↓
GitHub Project / Executor / Result
```

A graph may represent a workflow such as:

```text
Load Project
     ↓
Select Task
     ↓
Inspect Resources
     ↓
Choose Execution Path
   ┌────────┴────────┐
Claude            GitWeave
   └────────┬────────┘
          Result
            ↓
Update Project
```

The purpose is not to hard-code this specific flow, but to make comparable project-level workflows explicit and executable as graphs.

## 1. Use GitHub Project as the canonical project state

Use GitHub Projects as the first project backend.

Do not introduce a separate ProjectWeave task database or project-management database.

Reuse existing GitHub primitives wherever practical:

```text
GitHub Project → Project
Issue          → Task
Pull Request   → Proposed result
Status         → Task state
Priority       → Task priority
Label / Field  → Classification / eligibility
Comment        → Execution result / diagnostic
Git            → Artifacts and source history
```

ProjectWeave should read project state from GitHub and reflect relevant operations back to GitHub.

Do not distribute canonical project state across ProjectWeave-specific Git refs or Git notes in this first design.

GitWeave uses Git naturally for execution artifacts and provenance. ProjectWeave has a different responsibility: GitHub Project should remain the human-visible canonical project state.

## 2. Define project-level workflows as graphs

ProjectWeave should accept a graph definition and execute it.

The initial graph model should support at least:

- nodes
- execution order
- structured data handoff between nodes
- conditional routing

Additional control flow such as loops may be added if it is required by the Issue #1 use cases.

Do not add graph features only because they may be useful in the future. Keep the initial graph model to the smallest set of primitives actually needed.

## 3. Keep the node model small

Do not create a large family of specialized node types for task-specific roles.

Avoid designs such as:

```text
SelectIssueNode
PlanningNode
ReviewNode
FixNode
DocumentationNode
```

unless a role is genuinely a runtime concept rather than task-specific behavior.

Study the graph/runtime design in [GitWeave](https://github.com/takahirox/gitweave) and reuse relevant lessons.

GitWeave intentionally keeps its runtime concepts small:

- planner, worker, reviewer, and fixer are not distinct runtime node types
- they are ordinary Agent Nodes configured by instruction and options
- runtime-owned operations are represented separately as explicit System Actions
- control flow is represented by the graph rather than specialized agent roles

ProjectWeave should investigate whether the same principle applies at the project level:

> Before adding a specialized node type, prefer expressing task-specific behavior through instructions, configuration, structured inputs/results, and graph composition when possible.

The goal is not to copy GitWeave directly. ProjectWeave has different responsibilities, especially project-level orchestration and AI resource constraints.

## 4. Allow project operations from the graph

The graph should be able to observe and operate on GitHub Project state.

The first end-to-end use case needs at least the ability to:

- read Project items
- identify eligible tasks
- read Priority / Status or equivalent metadata
- select a task
- reflect execution results back to the Issue / Project

Whether these become generic nodes, System Actions, or another small primitive should be decided during implementation in favor of the simplest coherent model.

## 5. Treat the Resource Envelope as a first-class Run input

A Run should receive the AI resources available to this project from outside ProjectWeave.

For example:

```text
Codex:
  available: 20

Claude:
  available: 40

API:
  budget_usd: 25
```

The first implementation does not need to query real subscription services automatically.

It is sufficient to provide the Resource Envelope explicitly as Run input.

Graph execution must be able to inspect resource state and use it for control flow.

For example:

```text
Claude resource available
        ↓ yes
     Claude
        ↓
     Execute

        no
        ↓
     GitWeave
        ↓
     Execute
```

Resource limits should be enforceable as hard constraints where appropriate. Execution must not use a resource that is unavailable under the supplied envelope.

Do not implement advanced resource optimization in this issue.

The goal is to establish the core model:

> Resource state is an explicit control input to graph execution.

## 6. Keep executors separate from ProjectWeave

ProjectWeave should not implement task-solving intelligence itself.

Conceptually:

```text
ProjectWeave
     ↓
Executor boundary
     ↓
GitWeave / Claude / Codex / ...
```

An executor receives a task/request and returns a result.

The first implementation should support at least one real executor. GitWeave is a primary candidate for the first executor.

ProjectWeave core must not become tightly coupled to GitWeave internals.

Do not build a general-purpose plugin framework. Define only the smallest executor boundary required by the first real integrations.

## 7. Return executor results to the graph

Executor output should return to ProjectWeave as structured result data that downstream nodes can use.

For example:

```text
Execute
  output:
    status
    message
    references
        ↓
Evaluate / Update Project
```

Task-specific semantic interpretation should not be hard-coded into the runtime.

## 8. Reflect results back into GitHub

Project-level outcomes should be represented with existing GitHub primitives wherever practical.

Examples include:

- Issue comments
- Issue / Project status
- Priority or custom fields
- Pull Request references
- execution failure information

Do not introduce a ProjectWeave-specific history database in the first implementation.

A human looking at GitHub should be able to understand the current project and task state.

## 9. Run one graph execution from the CLI

The first runtime does not need to be a long-running service.

A command such as:

```text
projectweave run --graph GRAPH --project PROJECT --resources RESOURCES
```

should execute one graph Run and then exit.

Scheduler, daemon, cron, and webhook support can be added later.

This keeps the runtime independently testable and avoids unnecessary service infrastructure.

## Initial end-to-end example

At minimum, the implementation should be able to run a graph like:

```text
GitHub Project
      ↓
Load eligible Issues
      ↓
Select highest-priority Task
      ↓
Inspect Resource Envelope
      ↓
Choose Execution Path
   ┌─────────┴─────────┐
Claude               GitWeave
   └─────────┬─────────┘
           Result
             ↓
Update GitHub Issue / Project
```

A single Run should therefore be able to:

1. read a GitHub Project
2. load eligible tasks
3. select one task
4. inspect the Resource Envelope
5. route graph execution based on resource state
6. invoke an executor
7. receive its result
8. reflect the result back to GitHub

## Design reference: GitWeave

Before and during implementation, study [GitWeave](https://github.com/takahirox/gitweave) for relevant design lessons, especially:

- graph validation
- separation of Agent Nodes and System Actions
- generic Agent Nodes configured through instructions
- structured results
- data handoff between nodes
- conditional and loop control flow
- separation of Runtime Failures and task outcomes
- bounded execution
- Run records and provenance
- CLI graph execution

Distinguish ideas that transfer cleanly from those that need different treatment at the project level.

In particular, GitWeave's principle of keeping runtime concepts small and leaving task intelligence in instructions and graph composition should be treated as a strong design reference.

ProjectWeave should not assume that GitWeave's Git commit/ref/note provenance model is also the right model for canonical project state. ProjectWeave's first backend should use GitHub Project as that canonical state.

## Success criteria

This issue is complete when ProjectWeave can:

- use a GitHub Project as the project backend
- define a project-level workflow as a graph
- execute that graph once from the CLI
- load tasks from GitHub Project / Issues
- select a task inside graph execution
- accept a Resource Envelope as Run input
- use resource state in graph control flow
- invoke an executor from the graph
- pass executor results to downstream nodes
- reflect results back to GitHub Project / Issue
- keep ProjectWeave core independent of a specific executor
- operate without a ProjectWeave-specific task database

## Design principles

In addition to Issue #1, the first implementation should:

- choose the smallest useful runtime concepts
- avoid specialized node types unless they are true runtime concepts
- reuse existing GitHub project primitives
- avoid reimplementing executor intelligence
- keep resource-allocation strategy outside the core
- preserve human-visible project state
- avoid abstractions added only for hypothetical future needs
- avoid subsystems until a concrete requirement exists
- reuse existing systems instead of rebuilding solved problems

## Out of scope

This issue does not include:

- UI
- daemon / scheduler / webhook support
- multi-project coordination
- automatic subscription-usage discovery
- advanced resource-allocation optimization
- automatic AI task creation
- an autonomous project-manager AI
- a custom Issue / Task management system
- a ProjectWeave-specific project-management database
- distributed scheduling
- multi-tenant service infrastructure
- a general-purpose plugin marketplace

- **Resource guarantees:** ProjectWeave should reject execution when the supplied Resource Envelope says the required resource is unavailable. Strict in-flight consumption enforcement is not guaranteed unless the executor exposes a mechanism that makes it possible.
- **Resource units:** do not force all resources into one universal unit. Each resource type should define its own accounting semantics.

This keeps the runtime small while still covering the core project-level orchestration model from Issue #1.

The next implementation step should be to document the minimal graph schema, Result / Failure contracts, GitHub Project mapping, and first executor adapter around these decisions, then implement the end-to-end CLI Run."
